title: Pod Stuck Terminating
brief: A stateful pod has been Terminating for 18 minutes. Investigate before considering force deletion.

commands.kubectl describe pod:
Node: worker-2 (NotReady)
Finalizers: kubernetes.io/pvc-protection
PreStop hook exceeded grace period

hints: Inspect deletion timestamps and finalizers.
Confirm whether the node and container runtime can report termination.
Force deletion removes the API object; it does not prove the process stopped.
diagnosis: The pod is blocked by an unreachable node, an incomplete preStop shutdown, and an attached persistent volume; force deletion could overlap the old stateful process with its replacement.
remediation: Restore or fence the node, verify the process is stopped and volume detached, resolve the finalizer blocker, then force-delete only as a last resort.
case_study: Force deletion removes the pod object immediately without confirming that the process stopped. Inspect events, finalizers, deletion timestamps, node health, runtime state, volume detachments, and shutdown behavior first.

title: CrashLoopBackOff Investigation
brief: A newly deployed API repeatedly crashes after starting.
objectives: Compare configuration with the last release

commands.kubectl describe pod:
Last State: Terminated; Exit Code: 1
Back-off restarting failed container

hints: Start with status and describe.
Previous logs survive the last container crash.
Check config, command, probes, and dependencies.
diagnosis: The new revision starts without DB_HOST and exits, producing CrashLoopBackOff.
remediation: Correct the configuration reference or roll back, then watch rollout status and logs.
case_study: A strong process is get pods, describe, current/previous logs, inspect spec/config, test dependencies, then compare revisions.

title: Rollout Followed by 502
brief: A Deployment completed, but users receive 502 responses.
hints: A 502 often means the proxy selected a backend but could not use it.
Trace Ingress → Service → Endpoint → container.
Compare targetPort with the listening port.
diagnosis: The Service sends traffic to targetPort 3000 while the new application listens on 8080.
remediation: Correct targetPort to 8080 and validate endpoint connectivity before completing rollout.
case_study: Successful rollout means Kubernetes reached desired state; it does not guarantee the traffic path is correct.

title: Service-to-Service Failure
brief: A pod works locally but cannot connect to the payments Service.

commands.kubectl get svc -A: payments service exists in namespace billing

hints: Local success does not validate DNS or network policy.
Short Service names resolve inside the same namespace.
Use payments.billing.svc.cluster.local.
diagnosis: The caller uses the namespace-local name payments, but the Service exists in billing; cross-namespace traffic also requires allowed policy.
remediation: Use the qualified DNS name and explicitly allow the traffic in NetworkPolicy.
case_study: Isolate name resolution, endpoint selection, port reachability, policy, and application behavior as separate layers.

title: Healthy Pods, No Endpoints
brief: A Service exists and pods look healthy, but its endpoint list is empty.
hints: Services select only matching pods in their namespace.
Running is not always Ready.
Here, the selector is singular while the label is plural.
diagnosis: The Service selector app=order does not match the pod label app=orders, so no endpoints are created.
remediation: Align selectors and labels, then confirm EndpointSlice population.
case_study: Empty endpoints usually point to selector mismatch, readiness failure, wrong namespace, or manual EndpointSlice issues.

title: Probe-Created Outage
brief: Aggressive health probes cause a slow-starting API to restart continuously.

commands.kubectl describe pod: Liveness failed: connection refused; Restart Count: 12

hints: Readiness controls traffic; liveness restarts; startup delays the other two.
A slow healthy startup should not fail liveness.
Add a startup probe sized to worst-case initialization.
diagnosis: Liveness runs during normal startup and repeatedly kills the container before it can become ready.
remediation: Add a startupProbe with adequate failureThreshold/periodSeconds and keep readiness and liveness focused on their distinct purposes.
case_study: Bad probes can turn slowness into an outage through restart storms or route traffic before dependencies are ready.

title: Stuck Deployment Rollout
brief: A rollout has not progressed and is nearing its deadline.

commands.kubectl rollout status: Waiting for deployment rollout: 1 of 3 updated replicas available

hints: A Deployment delegates pods to ReplicaSets.
Find the new ReplicaSet and its pods.
Events often expose scheduling, image, or probe failures.
diagnosis: The new ReplicaSet references an unavailable image, preventing updated pods from becoming available and stalling rollout.
remediation: Publish/fix the image or roll back; then monitor rollout status and availability.
case_study: Inspect Deployment conditions, ReplicaSets, pods, events, quotas, probes, and PDB constraints.

title: Node NotReady
brief: A worker becomes NotReady while running customer workloads.
objectives: Check kubelet, runtime, disk, and network

commands.kubectl describe node: Ready Unknown; Kubelet stopped posting node status; DiskPressure Unknown
commands.journalctl: kubelet: failed to contact API server; containerd healthy

hints: Existing processes may keep running despite control-plane uncertainty.
Controllers wait through toleration/eviction timing.
Check host services and connectivity.
diagnosis: Worker-3 cannot reach the API server, so kubelet heartbeats stop; pods may still run locally but are eventually evicted and replaced according to tolerations.
remediation: Restore node-to-control-plane connectivity, verify kubelet/runtime/resources, or safely drain/fence the node.
case_study: NotReady is a control-plane observation, not proof every container instantly stopped.

title: Pending Despite Free Resources
brief: A pod stays Pending although dashboards show spare CPU and memory.

commands.kubectl describe pod: 0/3 nodes: 2 node(s) didn't match node affinity, 1 had untolerated taint dedicated=gpu
commands.kubectl get nodes --show-labels: workers labeled zone=a; pod requires zone=b

hints: Scheduling considers more than resources.
Read FailedScheduling reasons.
Affinity and taints exclude all nodes here.
diagnosis: Required zone=b affinity matches no worker, and the remaining GPU node has an untolerated taint.
remediation: Correct the placement rule, label/add eligible capacity, or add a justified toleration.
case_study: Other blockers include unbound PVCs, host ports, topology spread, quotas, and scheduler profiles.

title: OOM and CPU Throttling
brief: A service alternates between restarts and high latency under load.

commands.kubectl describe pod: Requests cpu=250m memory=256Mi; Limits cpu=500m memory=512Mi; Last State OOMKilled

hints: Requests influence scheduling and CPU share.
Memory limit breach can kill; CPU limit generally throttles.
Look at working-set trends and latency.
diagnosis: The process exceeds its 512Mi memory limit and is OOMKilled while its 500m CPU limit throttles processing under load.
remediation: Fix leaks/usage, size requests and limits from metrics, and load-test changes.
case_study: Requests reserve scheduling capacity; limits constrain runtime consumption, with different consequences for CPU and memory.

title: Two Replicas, Still Downtime
brief: A two-replica API briefly goes offline during each deployment.

commands.kubectl describe pod: readiness path /ping returns 200 during cache warmup

hints: Replicas alone do not guarantee availability.
One unavailable replica plus one falsely Ready replica can mean zero capacity.
Check topology and disruption protection.
diagnosis: The rollout permits one pod down while the new pod reports Ready before it can serve traffic; both replicas also share one node.
remediation: Use meaningful readiness, suitable surge/unavailable values, topology spread/anti-affinity, and a PDB for voluntary disruptions.
case_study: Availability depends on readiness correctness, rollout math, capacity, and independent failure domains.

title: Rollout Capacity Controls
brief: Choose rollout settings for a four-replica latency-sensitive service.
symptoms: Cluster can temporarily host one extra pod

commands.kubectl rollout status: 1 old replica removed before replacement became Ready

hints: maxUnavailable bounds how many desired replicas may be unavailable.
maxSurge bounds temporary pods above desired count.
Zero unavailable and one surge prioritizes availability.
diagnosis: The current 25% maxUnavailable allows one of four replicas to be unavailable during rollout.
remediation: Use maxUnavailable=0 and maxSurge=1 if capacity supports it, with correct readiness and progress deadlines.
case_study: Percentages round differently: surge rounds up and unavailable rounds down.

title: Choose the Workload Controller
brief: Match five workloads to Kubernetes controllers.
objectives: Avoid using one controller for everything

commands.kubectl get deployments,statefulsets,dae: api Deployment; db StatefulSet; collector DaemonSet; migrate Job; backup CronJob

hints: Deployments manage interchangeable replicas.
StatefulSets preserve identity; DaemonSets target nodes.
Jobs finish; CronJobs schedule Jobs.
diagnosis: Use Deployment for API, StatefulSet for database, DaemonSet for node agent, Job for migration, and CronJob for nightly backup.
remediation: Apply controller-specific update, storage, and retry policies.
case_study: The controller should match identity, placement, completion, and scheduling needs.

title: Database Identity and Storage
brief: A replicated database was deployed with a Deployment and shared storage, causing identity confusion.

commands.kubectl get pods: db-7fc-x9 random name; db-7fc-z2 random name

hints: Databases often require stable ordinal identities.
volumeClaimTemplates give per-pod claims.
StatefulSet does not replace database replication design.
diagnosis: A Deployment provides interchangeable identities and the replicas improperly share one volume; the database requires stable identity and per-replica storage.
remediation: Use a StatefulSet with headless Service and volumeClaimTemplates plus database-aware replication, backups, and safe update policy.
case_study: StatefulSet is usually appropriate, but application-level consistency and failover remain the database's responsibility.

title: PVC Pending
brief: A database pod cannot schedule because its claim remains Pending.

commands.kubectl describe pvc: waiting for a volume to be created by provisioner fast.csi.local

hints: Describe the claim first.
Dynamic provisioning depends on StorageClass and CSI provisioner.
The referenced provisioner is not installed.
diagnosis: The PVC requests fast-rwo, whose CSI provisioner is absent, so no matching volume can be created or bound.
remediation: Use a valid StorageClass or install/repair the correct CSI driver; also verify capacity, modes, and topology.
case_study: Pending PVCs commonly involve missing class/provisioner, no matching PV, topology, capacity, or access-mode mismatch.

title: Internal DNS Failure
brief: A container resolves public domains but not cluster Service names.

commands.kubectl exec: nslookup example.com succeeds; nslookup api.default.svc.cluster.local times out

hints: External success does not prove cluster DNS works.
Cluster pods normally use ClusterFirst.
This pod inherited the node resolver.
diagnosis: dnsPolicy Default points the pod at an external resolver that does not know cluster.local records.
remediation: Use ClusterFirst unless host networking or a special DNS configuration justifies another policy.
case_study: Also inspect CoreDNS health/config, kube-dns Service, search domains, ndots, and UDP/TCP 53 policy.

title: Expose the Application
brief: Choose the right exposure mechanism for internal and external consumers.

commands.kubectl get svc: api ClusterIP; debug NodePort; public LoadBalancer

hints: ClusterIP is internal virtual IP.
NodePort opens a port on nodes; LoadBalancer asks an integration for an external balancer.
Ingress provides HTTP routing through a controller.
diagnosis: Use ClusterIP for internal access, NodePort mainly as a building block/debug option, LoadBalancer for direct external Service exposure, and Ingress for shared HTTP routing.
remediation: Select the least exposed mechanism and ensure an Ingress controller exists.
case_study: Ingress is an API object plus controller, not a Service type or automatic load balancer by itself.

title: Trace the Ingress Request
brief: Requests reach the controller but never succeed at the application.
hints: Trace DNS/LB → controller → rule → Service → Endpoint → container.
The endpoint advertises one port while Service targetPort names another.
Test each hop from an appropriate network location.
diagnosis: The Service targets 8080 although the application endpoint listens on 3000, so the controller cannot connect upstream.
remediation: Correct targetPort and validate with controller logs, endpoints, and in-cluster curl.
case_study: Also check class, hostname, path rewriting, TLS, readiness, EndpointSlices, policies, and controller-specific annotations.

title: NetworkPolicy Blocks Database
brief: Database calls time out immediately after a default-deny policy is introduced.
hints: NetworkPolicy is additive but default-deny changes the baseline.
Both source egress and destination ingress may need allowance.
Permit DNS and database TCP explicitly.
diagnosis: The app's egress permits only DNS and the database has default-deny ingress, so TCP/5432 is denied in both directions.
remediation: Add selector-scoped app egress and database ingress rules for TCP/5432 while retaining default deny.
case_study: Validate CNI policy support and test from the actual source pod; policy objects alone do not prove enforcement behavior.

title: ConfigMap Change Surprise
brief: A ConfigMap was updated, but application behavior did not change.
hints: Environment variables are fixed when the container starts.
Mounted ConfigMap files update eventually, but apps may not reload them.
A ConfigMap edit does not automatically create a Deployment rollout.
diagnosis: The ConfigMap is consumed through environment variables, so existing containers retain the old value until recreated.
remediation: Trigger a controlled rollout, or use checksum annotations/reloader patterns with readiness protection.
case_study: Even projected-volume updates do not guarantee the application notices or safely reloads changed content.

title: Zero-Downtime Secret Rotation
brief: Rotate database credentials while keeping all API replicas available.
symptoms: Pods read Secret through env vars
Database can temporarily accept two credentials
hints: Use an overlap window when the dependency supports it.
Secret env values require pod recreation.
Do not revoke the old credential before all consumers switch.
diagnosis: Updating or revoking one in-place credential can leave old replicas unable to connect during the rollout.
remediation: Create new credential, publish a versioned Secret, roll pods gradually, validate connections, then revoke and remove the old credential.
case_study: Rotation safety comes from dual validity/versioning, rollout controls, readiness, monitoring, and rollback capability.

title: ServiceAccount and RBAC
brief: Explain how a pod identity receives Kubernetes API permissions.
hints: ServiceAccount is workload identity.
RBAC Roles/ClusterRoles define permissions.
Bindings connect subjects to those permissions.
diagnosis: The reporter ServiceAccount identifies the pod, while its RoleBinding grants the pod-reader Role permissions in the namespace.
remediation: Grant only required verbs/resources and verify with kubectl auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:namespace:name.
case_study: A ServiceAccount has no broad power merely by existing; bindings determine authorization.

title: Forbidden Kubernetes API
brief: A controller receives Forbidden when attempting to patch Deployments.

commands.kubectl logs: deployments.apps is forbidden: serviceaccount ops:releaser cannot patch resource deployments

hints: Forbidden is authorization, not authentication.
Parse verb, API group, resource, namespace, and user from the error.
The Role lacks patch.
diagnosis: The ServiceAccount is bound correctly, but its Role permits only get/list/watch and lacks patch on apps/deployments.
remediation: Add only the required patch permission in the correct namespace and retest with impersonation.
case_study: kubectl auth can-i and binding inspection are safer than guessing or granting a broad role.

title: The cluster-admin Shortcut
brief: A developer proposes cluster-admin to resolve an application's Forbidden error.
symptoms: Application needs to read one ConfigMap
hints: cluster-admin can mutate nearly all cluster resources and RBAC.
A compromised pod inherits its bound permissions.
Grant get on the named resource/namespace instead.
diagnosis: cluster-admin would turn an application compromise into full cluster takeover for a single missing ConfigMap read permission.
remediation: Create a namespaced Role with get on configmaps, optionally restrict resourceNames, and bind it to the ServiceAccount.
case_study: RBAC escalation should solve the exact denied action, not silence authorization controls.

title: Security Context vs RBAC
brief: A pod cannot write a volume and also cannot list Kubernetes Secrets. Identify the separate controls.
objectives: Separate OS/container controls from API authorization
Choose the right fix for each
hints: Security contexts control process/container privileges and filesystem identity.
RBAC authorizes Kubernetes API requests.
Neither substitutes for the other.
diagnosis: The volume write failure is an ownership/security-context issue, while Secret listing is independently denied by RBAC.
remediation: Correct volume permissions/fsGroup or CSI behavior, and grant only API permissions genuinely required.
case_study: Do not grant cluster-admin or run privileged to solve unrelated layers.

title: Placement Rules
brief: A workload must prefer SSD nodes, tolerate dedicated nodes, and spread replicas.
hints: nodeSelector is simple required label matching.
Affinity offers required/preferred and pod relationships.
Toleration permits but does not attract placement.
diagnosis: The workload tolerates dedicated nodes but lacks affinity/topology rules, so the scheduler may co-locate replicas.
remediation: Use SSD node affinity, justified toleration, and pod anti-affinity or topology spread across hosts/zones.
case_study: Taints repel; tolerations permit; selectors/affinity attract or require.

title: What a PDB Protects
brief: Define protection for a three-replica API during voluntary disruptions.
hints: PDB limits simultaneous voluntary evictions.
It affects operations such as drain.
It does not prevent crashes, node loss, OOM, or bad deployments.
diagnosis: minAvailable=2 allows one voluntary disruption while three healthy replicas exist, but cannot guarantee availability during involuntary failures.
remediation: Combine PDB with replicas, topology, readiness, capacity, and sound rollout settings.
case_study: A PDB is an eviction constraint, not a universal high-availability mechanism.

title: PDB Blocks Maintenance
brief: kubectl drain hangs because an application cannot be evicted.

commands.kubectl drain: Cannot evict pod as it would violate the pod's disruption budget

hints: The PDB correctly prevents voluntary unavailability.
Create another healthy replica if the application supports it.
Verify capacity and topology before retrying.
diagnosis: A single-replica workload with minAvailable=1 has zero allowed disruptions, so drain cannot evict it.
remediation: Scale to at least two healthy replicas or arrange an approved maintenance window and deliberate budget change.
case_study: PDBs can expose architecture that cannot tolerate planned maintenance; bypassing them transfers risk to users.

title: HPA Does Not Scale
brief: CPU is high but the HorizontalPodAutoscaler remains at two replicas.
objectives: Check resource requests and scale target

commands.kubectl describe hpa: FailedGetResourceMetric: missing request for cpu in container sidecar
commands.kubectl get deployment -o yaml: api requests cpu=250m; sidecar has no cpu request

hints: Utilization targets depend on resource requests.
Inspect HPA conditions and events.
Every relevant container needs a CPU request for pod utilization.
diagnosis: The sidecar has no CPU request, so HPA cannot calculate pod CPU utilization and reports an unknown metric.
remediation: Set evidence-based CPU requests for containers and verify metrics, HPA conditions, min/max, and stabilization behavior.
case_study: Also check Metrics Server/APIService, target name, metric type, readiness, and scaling policies.

title: Metrics Server Outage
brief: The resource metrics API becomes unavailable during peak traffic.
hints: Metrics Server supplies resource metrics, not pod execution.
HPA cannot make normal resource-metric decisions without data.
Existing replicas are not automatically killed.
diagnosis: Metrics Server has no endpoints, making resource metrics unavailable; HPA cannot calculate desired replica count and current pods remain at their last scale.
remediation: Restore Metrics Server/APIService and validate kubelet connectivity/certificates; monitor capacity manually meanwhile.
case_study: Behavior is subject to HPA controller safeguards, but loss of metrics removes responsive autoscaling.

title: Safe Node Drain
brief: Prepare a worker for kernel maintenance without unnecessary downtime.

commands.kubectl drain: warning: ignoring DaemonSet-managed Pods; evicting api-7cc
commands.kubectl get pods -o wide: replacement api pod Ready on worker-1

hints: Cordon prevents new scheduling.
Drain uses eviction and should respect PDBs.
DaemonSets and local data need explicit handling.
diagnosis: The node can be maintained after cordoning, draining managed pods with appropriate flags, and verifying replacements and volume detachments.
remediation: Run cordon, review workloads/PDBs/local storage, drain, verify health, maintain, then uncordon.
case_study: Avoid force flags until you understand unmanaged pods, emptyDir loss, DaemonSets, and stateful detach behavior.

title: Drain Refuses Eviction
brief: Node drain stops on several special-case pods.

commands.kubectl drain: cannot delete DaemonSet pod; cannot delete pod with local storage; pod not managed; eviction violates PDB
commands.kubectl get pod -o wide: agent owner=DaemonSet; debug owner=<none>; cache uses emptyDir

hints: Drain avoids data loss and unmanaged workload deletion by default.
DaemonSets remain by design when ignored.
Static pods cannot be removed through API eviction.
diagnosis: Drain is blocked by an unmanaged local-data pod and PDB, while DaemonSet/static pods require special handling rather than ordinary eviction.
remediation: Review data and ownership, restore PDB headroom, replace unmanaged pods with controllers, and use flags only with understood consequences.
case_study: Refusal is a safety signal, not merely a command inconvenience.

title: Protecting etcd
brief: Explain what must be recovered after catastrophic control-plane data loss.
symptoms: Workers may still run old workloads
hints: etcd stores authoritative Kubernetes API state.
It includes workloads, configuration, RBAC, and Secret objects.
Backups are useful only if restorable and protected.
diagnosis: Loss of etcd means loss of cluster desired state and metadata, even if some containers keep running on workers.
remediation: Take encrypted, off-cluster snapshots on schedule and test version-compatible restoration with certificates and encryption keys.
case_study: Container images and persistent application volumes do not reconstruct Kubernetes control-plane state.

title: API Server Unavailable
brief: Workers remain up, but all API servers are unreachable.
symptoms: No new scheduling or reconciliation occurs
hints: Running containers and kube-proxy/CNI state may continue locally.
Controllers and scheduler depend on the API.
Desired-state changes and many recovery actions stop.
diagnosis: Existing workloads may continue serving with cached networking, but scheduling, reconciliation, scaling, rollouts, leases, and administrative changes are impaired without the API server.
remediation: Restore the API/control-plane path urgently and verify etcd, certificates, load balancer, and component health.
case_study: The cluster does not instantly stop, but it loses its control loop and becomes increasingly stale and fragile.

title: One HA Control Plane Fails
brief: One of three control-plane nodes fails in an HA cluster.
symptoms: API load balancer has two healthy backends

commands.kubectl get nodes: cp-1 Ready; cp-2 Ready; cp-3 NotReady

hints: Three-member etcd tolerates one failure.
The load balancer must remove the failed API endpoint.
Do not take another member down before restoring redundancy.
diagnosis: The cluster remains functional because API endpoints and etcd retain a healthy majority, but it has lost fault tolerance.
remediation: Confirm quorum and load-balancer routing, repair/replace the failed member carefully, and return to three healthy members.
case_study: HA depends on independent failure domains and maintained quorum, not merely three machine names.

title: App Failure or Cluster Network?
brief: Requests between two services fail intermittently. Determine the failing layer.
symptoms: One pod fails direct health checks
objectives: Test at pod, endpoint, and Service layers

commands.kubectl get events: no CNI or node network warnings

hints: Bypass the Service and test each endpoint.
A 500 is an application response, unlike timeout/reset routing symptoms.
Correlate failures to a pod, node, zone, or all traffic.
diagnosis: Only one endpoint returns an application-generated 500 due to database pool exhaustion; Service routing and pod networking work.
remediation: Remove the bad pod via readiness, fix pool handling, and monitor per-endpoint health.
case_study: Layered tests prevent blaming Kubernetes for an application that is reachable but unhealthy.

title: Describe vs Logs
brief: A pod will not start, but kubectl logs returns no output.

commands.kubectl logs: Error: container is waiting to start
commands.kubectl describe pod:
FailedMount: secret tls-cert not found
Node: worker-1
QoS Class: Burstable
Conditions: PodScheduled=True

hints: Logs are application/container stdout and stderr.
Describe includes events, conditions, state/reasons, mounts, probes, requests, and scheduling details.
Pre-start failures may produce no container logs.
diagnosis: The container never starts because a referenced Secret cannot mount; describe exposes the kubelet event that logs cannot contain.
remediation: Create/fix the Secret reference and use both describe and logs according to the failing lifecycle stage.
case_study: Describe summarizes API status and recent events; logs show what a started container emitted.

title: Previous Container Logs
brief: The current container is starting normally, but the prior instance crashed.

commands.kubectl logs --previous: panic: nil pointer in payment handler

hints: Use the previous flag.
For multi-container pods, add -c container-name.
Node log rotation means this is not durable centralized logging.
diagnosis: The relevant crash evidence is in the previous container instance and shows an application panic with exit code 2.
remediation: Use kubectl logs POD -c CONTAINER --previous, then fix the panic and rely on centralized logs for durable history.
case_study: --previous typically retrieves the immediately preceding terminated instance, not an unlimited restart archive.

title: Ephemeral Debug Container
brief: A distroless production container has no shell, curl, or DNS tools.
symptoms: Image cannot be rebuilt during incident

commands.kubectl exec: exec: sh: executable file not found

hints: Ephemeral containers add troubleshooting tools to an existing pod.
They share selected namespaces but are not ordinary app containers.
Use approved images and audit access.
diagnosis: The minimal image is healthy by design but lacks tools; an ephemeral debug container is appropriate for inspecting its network/process context.
remediation: Use kubectl debug with an approved image and target, collect evidence, then fix the underlying issue without bloating production images.
case_study: Use a copied debug pod when changing commands, filesystem, or isolation is safer than touching the live pod.

title: Roll Back or Roll Forward
brief: A production release causes checkout errors. Decide the safest recovery path.
symptoms: New release includes backward-compatible schema change
objectives: Know when a forward fix is safer

commands.kubectl get job: schema migration completed; additive column only

hints: Rollback when impact is high and previous state is safe/reversible.
Roll forward when rollback is unsafe due to irreversible state/schema/API changes or a tiny verified fix is faster.
Disablement/feature flags may be fastest.
diagnosis: The release has severe impact, the prior version is known good, and the database change is backward-compatible, so rollback or feature disablement is safer than debugging live.
remediation: Stop impact with the rehearsed rollback/flag, verify metrics, then repair and redeploy; roll forward only if compatibility or data changes make rollback unsafe.
case_study: The decision is risk-based: user impact, time to recovery, confidence, data compatibility, and reversibility matter more than ideology.
